source_refs.note: Exercise 2.1, Question 12: differentiate y = sin^3(cos 2v) w.r.t. v; book p. 41. Unit 2 has no printed answers.

blocks.explanation:
The variable is \(v\). \(y = [\sin(\cos 2v)]^3\) has four layers: cube, sine, cosine, \(2v\).
The chain rule is applied once for each layer, from the outside in.
Plan: substitutions \(w = 2v\), \(u = \cos w\), \(s = \sin u\), \(y = s^3\); multiply the four derivatives.
steps:
Given: \(y = \sin^3(\cos 2v)\).
To find: \(\frac{dy}{dv}\).
Method: chain rule through four layers.

Name the layers
\[w = 2v,\ u = \cos w,\ s = \sin u,\ y = s^3\]
Why: \(\sin^3(\cdot)\) means \([\sin(\cdot)]^3\); each layer is a basic function.

Derivative of each layer
\[\dfrac{dy}{ds} = 3s^2,\quad \dfrac{ds}{du} = \cos u\]
\[\dfrac{du}{dw} = -\sin w,\quad \dfrac{dw}{dv} = 2\]
Why: power rule, \((\sin)' = \cos\), \((\cos)' = -\sin\), \((2v)' = 2\).

Put the layers back
\[= 3\sin^2(\cos 2v)\cos(\cos 2v)\]
\[\quad \times (-\sin 2v)(2)\]
\[= -6\sin 2v\,\sin^2(\cos 2v)\cos(\cos 2v)\]
Why: \(s = \sin(\cos 2v)\), \(u = \cos 2v\), \(w = 2v\); \(3 \times 2 = 6\) with the minus sign.

Check at v = 0
\[-6\sin 0 \cdots = 0\]
Why: \(\cos 2v\) has its maximum at \(v = 0\), so the inner layer is flat there and \(y\) must be flat too.
